241: Hill concludes Chapter 13 by stating that through repeated reading and mental stimulation, one will eventually possess a power enabling them to throw off discouragement, master fear, overcome procrastination, and draw freely upon imagination. Then one will have felt the touch of that unknown something which has been the moving spirit of every truly great thinker, leader, artist, musician, writer, scientist, or statesman. Then one will be in position to transmute DESIRES into their physical or financial counterpart as easily as one may lie down and quit at the first sign of opposition. Under 'Faith vs. Fear,' Hill states that previous chapters described how to develop FAITH through autosuggestion, desire, and the subconscious mind. The final pages will present detailed instructions for mastery of FEAR. Here will be found a full description of the six fears causing all discouragement, timidity, procrastination, indifference, indecision, and lack of ambition, self-reliance, initiative, self-control, and enthusiasm. He urges readers to search themselves carefully as they study these six enemies, as they may exist only in the subconscious mind, where their presence is hard to detect. The six fears are nothing but ghosts because they exist only in one's mind, yet ghosts—creations of uncontrolled imagination—have caused most of the damage people have done to their own minds.
242: This page features a single inspirational quote in large text: 'Without doubt, the most common weakness of all human beings is the habit of leaving their minds open to the negative influence of other people.' This quote serves as a thematic divider, introducing the concept that will be elaborated in the Epilogue—the danger of susceptibility to negative influences from others. The page bears the OceanofPDF.com watermark.
243: This page opens the Epilogue: 'HOW TO OUTWIT THE 6 GHOSTS OF FEAR—Take Inventory of Yourself As You Read This and Find Out How Many of the Ghosts Stand in Your Way.' Hill states that before putting any portion of the philosophy into successful use, the mind must be prepared to receive it. The preparation begins with study, analysis, and understanding of three enemies: INDECISION, DOUBT, and FEAR. The Sixth Sense will never function while any of these three negatives remain. They are closely tied—where one is found, the other two are close at hand. INDECISION is the seedling of FEAR. Indecision crystallizes DOUBT. The two blend and become FEAR. This blending process is often slow, which is why these enemies are so dangerous—they germinate and grow without being observed. The remainder of the chapter describes an end that must be attained before the philosophy can be put into practical use. It also analyzes a condition that has reduced large numbers to poverty, and states a truth that must be understood by all who would accumulate riches. Hill turns the spotlight on the cause and cure of the Six Basic Fears—before mastering an enemy, one must know its name, its habits, and its place of abode.
244: Hill presents 'The Six Basic Fears': named in order of most common appearance, they are: (1) The fear of POVERTY—at the heart of most people's worries; (2) The fear of CRITICISM; (3) The fear of ILL HEALTH; (4) The fear of LOSS OF LOVE OF SOMEONE; (5) The fear of OLD AGE; (6) The fear of DEATH. All other fears can be grouped under these six headings. The prevalence of these fears runs in cycles: during the Depression, the cycle of FEAR OF POVERTY; during World War I, FEAR OF DEATH; just after the war, FEAR OF ILL HEALTH (evidenced by worldwide epidemic). Fears are nothing more than states of mind, and one's state of mind is subject to control and direction. An individual can create nothing which he or she does not first conceive as an impulse of thought. Following this is the statement of still greater importance: THOUGHT IMPULSES BEGIN IMMEDIATELY TO TRANSLATE THEMSELVES INTO THEIR PHYSICAL EQUIVALENT, WHETHER THOSE THOUGHTS ARE VOLUNTARY OR INVOLUNTARY. Thought impulses picked up by chance from other minds may determine one's financial, business, professional, or social destiny just as surely as those created by intent and design.
245: Hill explains that all human beings have the ability to completely control their own mind, and with this control, can open their minds to 'tramp' thought impulses from others' brains or close the doors tightly and admit only impulses of their own choice. Nature has endowed human beings with absolute control over only one thing: THOUGHT. If ALL THOUGHT HAS A TENDENCY TO CLOTHE ITSELF IN ITS PHYSICAL EQUIVALENT (true beyond any doubt), then thought impulses of fear and poverty cannot be translated into terms of courage and financial gain. The people of America began thinking of poverty after the 1929 Wall Street crash; slowly that mass thought crystallized into its physical equivalent—the depression. This had to happen; it conforms to the laws of Nature. Under 'The Fear of Poverty,' Hill declares there can be no compromise between POVERTY and RICHES—the roads travel in opposite directions. If you want riches, you must refuse any circumstance leading toward poverty. 'Riches' is used in its broadest sense: financial, spiritual, mental, and material estates. The starting point of the path to riches is DESIRE.
246: Hill states that fear of poverty is a state of mind, nothing else, but it is sufficient to destroy one's chances of achievement in any undertaking. He provides a devastating catalog of its effects: it paralyzes the faculty of reason, destroys imagination, kills self-reliance, undermines enthusiasm, discourages initiative, leads to uncertainty of purpose, encourages procrastination, wipes out enthusiasm, makes self-control impossible. It takes the charm from one's personality, destroys accurate thinking, diverts concentration, kills persistence, turns willpower into nothingness, destroys ambition, beclouds memory, invites failure in every conceivable form. It kills love and assassinates the finer emotions of the heart, discourages friendship, invites disaster in a hundred forms, leads to sleeplessness, misery, and unhappiness—all despite the obvious truth that we live in a world of overabundance of everything the heart could desire, with nothing standing between us and our desires except lack of a definite purpose and plans deriving from it. The Fear of Poverty is the most destructive of the Six Basic Fears, placed at the head of the list because it is the most difficult to master. Considerable courage is required to state the truth about its origin, and still greater courage to accept the truth after it has been stated.
247: Hill traces the fear of poverty to human beings' inherited tendency to PREY UPON OTHERS ECONOMICALLY. Animals prey upon one another physically because their capacity to think is limited. Human beings, with superior sense of intuition and capacity to think and reason, do not eat others bodily—they get more satisfaction out of 'eating' them FINANCIALLY. Human beings are so avaricious that every conceivable law has been passed to safeguard them from each other. Our age is most characterized by 'money-madness'—people are considered less than dust unless they can display a fat bank account. But if they have money—never mind how acquired—they are 'royalty' or 'big shots,' above the law, ruling in politics and business. Nothing brings so much suffering and humility as POVERTY—only those who have experienced it understand the full meaning. People fear poverty because through inherited experience they have learned that some individuals cannot be trusted where money and earthly possessions are concerned. The majority of marriages continue to be motivated by wealth possessed by one or both parties—no wonder divorce courts stay busy. Hill prescribes self-analysis: one is both court and jury, prosecuting attorney and defense attorney, plaintiff and defendant—and it is YOU who are on trial. Face the facts squarely; ask definite questions and demand direct replies.
248: Hill instructs that if one cannot be an impartial judge in self-examination, call upon someone who knows you well to serve as judge. You are after the truth—get it no matter the cost, even if it temporarily embarrasses you. Most people, asked what they fear most, would reply 'I fear nothing'—an inaccurate reply because few realize they are bound, handicapped, and whipped spiritually and physically by some form of fear. So subtle and deeply seated is fear that one may go through life burdened with it, never recognizing its presence. Only a courageous analysis will disclose this universal enemy. Hill presents 'Symptoms of the Fear of Poverty': INDIFFERENCE—lack of ambition, willingness to tolerate poverty, mental and physical laziness, lack of initiative, imagination, enthusiasm and self-control. INDECISION—permitting others to do one's thinking, staying on the fence. DOUBT—expressed through alibis and excuses to cover up failures, envy of the successful, or criticism of them. WORRY—finding fault with others, spending beyond income, neglect of appearance, scowling, intemperance, nervousness, lack of poise and self-reliance. OVER-CAUTION—looking for the negative side of every circumstance, thinking and talking of possible failure, knowing all roads to disaster but never searching for plans to avoid failure, waiting for the 'right time' until waiting becomes a permanent habit.
249: Hill continues symptoms of the Fear of Poverty: PROCRASTINATION—putting off until tomorrow what should have been done last year, spending enough time creating alibis to have done the job, refusal to accept responsibility, willingness to compromise rather than fight, compromising with difficulties instead of using them as steppingstones. Bargaining with life for a penny instead of demanding prosperity, opulence, riches, contentment, and happiness. Planning what to do IF AND WHEN OVERTAKEN BY FAILURE instead of BURNING ALL BRIDGES AND MAKING RETREAT IMPOSSIBLE. Weakness or total lack of self-confidence, definiteness of purpose, self-control, initiative, enthusiasm, ambition, thrift, and sound reasoning ability. EXPECTING POVERTY INSTEAD OF DEMANDING RICHES. Association with those who accept poverty instead of seeking the company of those who demand and receive riches. Under 'Money Talks!,' Hill anticipates the question 'Why did you write a book about money? Why measure riches in dollars alone?' He acknowledges there are other forms of riches more desirable than money, but millions of people will say, 'Give me all the money I need, and I will find everything else I want.' The major reason he wrote this book on money is that the world has but lately passed through an experience that left millions paralyzed with the FEAR OF POVERTY.
250: Hill quotes Westbrook Pegler from the New York World-Telegram at length, describing what fear of poverty does to a person. Pegler writes that money is only clam shells or metal discs or scraps of paper, and there are treasures of the heart and soul which money cannot buy, but most people, being broke, are unable to keep this in mind and sustain their spirits. When a man is down and out and on the street, unable to get any job, something happens to his spirit observable in the droop of his shoulders, the set of his hat, his walk and his gaze. He cannot escape a feeling of inferiority among people with regular employment, even though he knows they are not his equals in character, intelligence, or ability. Even his friends feel a sense of superiority and regard him, perhaps unconsciously, as a casualty. He may borrow for a time, but borrowing merely to live is a depressing experience, and the money lacks the power of earned money to revive his spirits. When a man is down and out he has time on his hands for brooding. He may travel miles to see a man about a job and discover it is filled or that it is one of those jobs with no base pay but only commission on selling some useless knickknack. He walks and walks, gazing into store windows at luxuries which are not for him, feeling inferior. With a little money he would be himself again.
